parent: (story) The plunging price of AI
text:
From the article:



AI has gotten cheaper more quickly than any other transformative technology in history. The cost of achieving a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023, or 13× per year. That price drop is four times faster than DNA sequencing, six times faster than compute, 18 times faster than lithium batteries, and (in the century up to 1973) 54 times faster than electricity.



[...]


The next chart shows some examples. On January 31, 2025, OpenAI released a new iteration in its series of “reasoning” models, called o3. We estimate that for an average cost of 30 cents per question, it could achieve a 75% score on GPQA Diamond, a multiple-choice exam covering PhD-level physics, chemistry, and biology.1 Just under 18 months later, OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Luna. It scored just as well — for four hundredths of a penny per question ($0.0004). That is a 725-fold drop in the price of thought in under 18 months. It is like the sticker price on a new car falling from $50,000 to $69. No other general-purpose technology in history appears to have gotten so cheap so fast.


[...]


Our analysis comes with major caveats. AI companies may be expressly training their models for some benchmarks (“benchmaxxing”), so that improvement on the benchmarks outstrips improvement for real-world tasks. Even if they are not, doing well on a benchmark is not synonymous with useful work. Because we focus on the frontier — the absolute cheapest model capable of any given level of performance — we implicitly posit an AI user who relentlessly searches for the most cost-effective model for each task, when real users do not switch models so often, and therefore do not reap quite the same savings. Our data are incomplete and noisy: the timeframe is barely three years, and we do not include all combinations of AI model and benchmark. Prices drop differently for different models, benchmarks, time periods, and performance ranges, and there are many reasonable ways to average over this variegated experience. Overall, while we believe that our bottom-line numbers are reasonably representative of reality, they should not be read as exact.

author: MimicSquid
parent: (story) Given everything we know about AI so far, what do you think it can or cannot be good for?
text:
First off, I'm not a sceptic or a believer, as "AI" is too broad a domain to just have one thought about it unless you're a fanatic one way or the other.

I think that for data sorting and discovery it can be great, especially when there's checks and balances to verify the outcome amd it's working with a stable data set that isn't trying to incorporate breaking news. "Review the files of this business that closed 12 years ago and give me the names of the employees and the document you used for that info." turns hours of manually searching through misfiled and poorly named files into a 3 minute task to confirm the findings. But when the data is in flux or it's largely based off of things that confident idiots said online it can spit out hallucinations and wrong information with great confidence. It's not a universally good tool.

For generative tasks, I think it does a decent job at spitting out pablum. Generic pop songs, overly shiny and complicated images, trite stories that don't go anywhere. But that's a trap. It only feeds on what humans make, and if we make it impossible for humans to make a living making art then we'll just have incestuous generations of ai generated content that feeds on itself. Beyond that, I enjoy art because it's saying something to me. It's an expression of another person, conveying something beyond the words, sounds, or images themselves. Generative art is like clip art or emoji. Maybe it's got a single big statement: "be afraid!" "be horny!" "spend money!" "OBEY!" but that's not an interesting level of art to engage with.

In the past, I have enjoyed some AI-generated things that were unintentionally funny, like Will Smith eating spaghetti, but those were the early days of gen AI when it wasn't so great at replicating its training data. That poor replication gave it some semblance of creativity. Now it's gotten so "good" that everything it makes is dull.

I guess its creations could be interesting from an anthropological or historical standpoint — like, here is the most generic example of this genre at this exact point in time, which might be a useful way to compare different genres or to study AI technology itself — but nothing I've seen gen AI create in the last couple of years has been very interesting for its own sake.

I think if gen AI were developed to be truly inventive, and not simply an attempted simulation of human creativity (which it will never be able to do as well as humans because it doesn't have human experiences to inform these choices), there might actually be some cool stuff it could do. Other kinds of AI, such as genetic algorithms, come up with some incredibly unique solutions to problems because they're not boxed in by trying to design the way a human designs — and so I find myself much more intrigued by what they create, despite being far older and far simpler than modern gen AI.

author: balooga
parent: (story) Given everything we know about AI so far, what do you think it can or cannot be good for?
text:
I disagree with the take that generative AI can’t create new art. I’ve spent enough time experimenting with diffusion tools and techniques to know that it absolutely can, in the hands of someone with a creative vision and an understanding of the tech. Because while models have been trained on existing art, and tend to seek a bland average of those weights, they can also be wrangled to synthesize entirely new constructs like nothing in their training data… because creativity doesn’t exist in a vacuum, it emerges from combining and subverting that which came before. Everything’s a remix.

Of course, the problem is the slop. We’re just completely swamped in bottom-of-the-barrel, low-effort garbage. I’m optimistic that after the novelty wears off, the deluge of slop will subside (somewhat). It may never go away. But I think the aesthetic we all associate with “AI art” today will go the way of those hyper-saturated tone-mapped HDR photographs that were all over Flickr 20 years ago. And in its wake we may see some new digital art movements that are really deliberately transformative and human-guided at every step. That’s my hope anyway. It’s hard to be optimistic about the future these days but I’m trying!

One novel use for AI that I’m actively researching is how to use it to turn low-quality book scans into high-quality accessible e-texts. If multimodal LLMs are able to perceptually interpret the semantic structure of an image of a page, they can reconstruct it as properly tagged document. I’m building a self-correcting diffusion+LLM loop to restore broken or washed-out glyphs in particularly bad scans, to infer he correct missing information that was never present in the original pixels. Much better than traditional OCR. I think there’s a ton of untapped potential in this application of AI and it could substantially improve the state of alternative formats for students with visual impairments or learning disabilities.

author: scarecrw
parent: (story) Given everything we know about AI so far, what do you think it can or cannot be good for?
text:
I'll share my 2¢ on a topic I've been thinking a lot about, informed by both my personal and professional experiences.

I'm optimistic about LLMs as learning tools, pessimistic about the current attempts at productizing this, and very doubtful that we'll see some miraculous revolution in education because of the technology. (I'm also concerned about how well institutions and students themselves are adapting to cheating with AI, but that's a different conversation)

I've had some fantastic experiences using LLMs myself as a learning aid both in topics I already have a background in and topics relatively new to me. When asking for explanations of topics heavily represented in its training data, it provides responses reaching the quality of some of the better textbook writing I've seen, and with the tremendous benefit of being able to direct the focus of the explanation at will. Paired with traditional resources, it's made for a productive, engaging learning experience.

I think I'm less concerned than most about hallucinations. For one, the current models are genuinely quite good when focusing on common topics. More than that, though, the issue of errors in educational materials is not unique to AI tools; take any heavily-marketed educational resource, give it to an expert, and they'll make swiss cheese poking holes in it. Cross-referencing information, using multiple sources, and simply testing ideas in the real world will continue to be important skills regardless of the educational medium.

With that said, I think there are a number of hurdles to overcome before this could impact broader education:


Knowing how to ask questions is hard and teaching the skill is tremendously challenging. I've seen the way some students interact with AI tools and you would need a tremendous amount of context to even guess as to what they were hoping to learn.

Structuring learning, especially as a beginner, is non-obvious. There's a phenomenon I've seen in education similar to the Peter principle where teachers are pushed to teach content as complex as they've ever mastered. In my experience, the best educators are those that know at least a few steps beyond the current level of their students such that they can tailor their instruction not to the current topic or the next, but to setting the student up for longer-term success. Tasking the student themselves to identify and order what they should learn extends this challenge even further.

Social pressure plays a way bigger role in education than we like to admit. There's something tantalizing about the idea that if we were all just left to our own devices and had access to the right tools we would have a world of genius autodidacts. It turns out most of us did our homework because our parents, teachers, and classmates told us we should. I'm strongly convinced that struggle is required for learning, and while AI tools may be able to replace humans as founts of knowledge, social motivation is a much harder problem to solve.


So I'm not sold on AI being the revolutionary solution to Bloom's 2 sigma problem, but if it can be a useful aid to those who know how to use it, and raise the floor for the expected level of quality in educational resources, I'd be happy.

Honestly... My prediction for ai usage in education is almost the exact opposite unfortunately.

From data I've seen about how students use AI, those predictions seem to be grounded in evidence.

The ultimate problem I think is that learning is like walking a tight rope. The process of understanding complex ideas  needs to be hard and uncomfortable. It needs to be hard enough that people come to realizations on their own from basic principles to really fundementally understand those ideas. At the same time, it needs to not be so hard that the student gets discouraged and gives up.

A good tutor is really adept at walking that tight rope. When a student asks why something is the way it is, the tutor won't just give them the answer, they'll point them in the direction they need to figure out the answer themselves, and nudge them in the right direction if any of their assumptions or deductions aren't correct, and explain why they aren't correct.

Publicly available AI tools aren't good at this part from what I've seen. They'll just straight up tell you the answer and praise you for asking it.

That causes that information to go in one ear and out another, because no work was done to arrive at the conclusion. From what we know about learning, that work and discomfort is just really vital to the process, and LLMs eliminate all the friction that causes it.

author: Berdes
parent: (story) Given everything we know about AI so far, what do you think it can or cannot be good for?
text:
I think there is a clear pattern where the usefulness of LLMs scales with how easily their output can be verified. The easiest being when the verification can be done automatically, such as code being compiled and tested or math proofs being checked with something like Lean. This will certainly speed up some tasks, but I doubt that most jobs consist of doing only that.

There are two things I have in mind where I think LLMs could be really useful tools that haven't been explored all that much so far (or at least I'm not aware of that). The first one is about proving software. A lot of bugs and security vulnerabilities come from stuff like buffer overflows, dereferencing null pointers and more generally invariants being violated. In my opinion, safer languages like Rust fall short on two aspects: they will rejects programs that are provably safe (sometimes trivially so) and they only check a small subset of issues with no way for programmers to extend what is being checked. More general approaches, where people can add verified annotation for any provable properties would be the logical next step. So far, this kind of approach was way too labor-intensive to make sense for almost all software, but I hope LLMs will help reduce this cost to make this approach more common.

The second thing that I think LLMs could help with is making interaction with complex software easier for casual users. As an example, I use Gimp every couple of months to do some basic image editing. Because of this low frequency, I will never build enough habit to be really efficient and I think that having an LLM translate human language into whatever the software understands could really help here. Importantly, I think that having a more structured output for the LLMs should reduce the risk of unwanted effects compared to asking a multimodal model.

On the other hand, hallucination and mistakes that basically no human would make are still a problem. For example, I recently had a model (I think GPT-6 Luna) casually drop something like "that was 17 months ago, so not quite a year" in the middle of an answer. I don't know if we will ever reach a point where this happens rarely enough that it won't affect the quality of outputs.

Clean room reverse engineering is legal, yes. It's widely understood that having the same people do the reversal as the implementation from the derived spec is a good way to get your ass sued into the ground. (This goes way back to things like the cloning of the IBM PC: one team with a test bench poking signals into the system and taking readings, and a fully separate team using their written spec to build a compatible BIOS.)

A straight decompile and port into another language would still be infringing (just as publishing a translation of a novel is infringing). Decompilation is one thing that you never want to do while doing legal reverse engineering, because you're exposing yourself to implementational details.

If no decompilation happened, we get into the untested minefield of "is a leak of the source or a decompilation in the training set?" That's a risk. Any indication that code is sufficiently similar will be used as evidence of infringement.

Regardless, an individual probably can't afford to be sued by Adobe in the first place. This is exactly the kind of case I've been waiting for (though my money was on a Microsoft product)...if this were to go to court, it could establish case law that will make LLM use scarier to lawyers than GPL software. (And then they'll find out that they were trained on GPL code and often emit it verbatim...)

author: creesch
parent: (story) Solo developer rebuilds Adobe Creative Suite in Rust using Claude, releases it free to all
text:
They can.


If you stretch the definition of "they can" then yes, they can. If you look at practical use, then for all intents and purposes they cannot.

Models perform worse with languages they have less training data for. Languages most common on GitHub like Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, etc generally show good performance where models score noticeably lower on things like Lua, R, Perl.

Frontier models tend to compensate for this by leaning on languages that look similar but that only goes as far. So no, if a language is not in the training data a model will not be able to work in it as fluently and, depending on the language struggle noticeably

Mind you, this is about languages they have been trained on. If they have no training data whatsoever for a language it will be even worse. Possibly you can compensate somewhat by having a prompt include "this language most closely relates to Y". But then you are also going to deal with a things like wrong assumptions about semantics, patterns that work slightly different causing issues, etc, etc.

Tool calls can help here but those are just a patch and will not yield the same results compared to a model natively having been trained on a language. It will also just mean more token consumption. And eat up a lot of your model's context window. Which matters more than you might realize as it is well documented that an advertised context window doesn't mean the model will perform as well with the entire window in use. Since there is no training data you'd need all relevant data always in that context window. Depending on the complexity this can mean a substantial use of the context window, resulting in additional degraded use. Improvements have been made here but this is also an area where open-weight models generally tend to trail behind, with a smaller effective context window than advertised.

So far I have just written about this in the context of one language even. Over times we are talking also about things like protocols, best practices, etc. Yes, you can put it all in tool calls, skills, etc. But again, that will not perform the same as the model having native base knowledge about a subject and at some point there will really be no effective context left to have it actually do the thing you want. You might say that it only needs to pull information in where it needs it, but if most of the project is something it has no data on that just means it has keep pulling in that data.

To sum it up, in the short term I'll hand it to you. Sure, small changes to frameworks and languages initially you'd be able to compensate for with some small degradation in performance. In the long term, no they effectively cannot.

As far as fine tuning goes, it effectively has a similar problem. Tuning is good at changing behavior and style, less so at adding new information to a model that was not included in pre-training. Knowledge added through fine tuning is something models tend to hallucinate more over, to the point that retrieval (so the earlier mentioned tool calls) is seen as more effective. Which, in itself already has limitations as I went over.

Fine tuning also tends to change models overall degrading some things they already "know" which only gets worse every time you tune a model again. Talking about years of drift and multiple fine tuning rounds and I guess you'll have the next generation meme about model rot the same way people meme about JPEG artifacts.

Then there is the practical aspect of it all. It is one thing to tune a model on one additional subject. That's not going to be the case though, it will not just be one language or one framework but all additional data and knowledge I already mentioned earlier. Even if fine tuning was without flaws it would be a massive undertaking to keep models up to date on all of that (or even a subset). As it stands fine tuning is not up to task of doing the same sort of training that these labs do. And no, the popular narrative that the Chinese labs are doing this with barely any budget isn't quite true.

Which returns me to my original point. Open weight models are also heavily subsidized at the moment, without millions invested in hardware to train these models it currently isn't possible to reproduce their results. And as I hopefully have made clear now, the current models will not remain usable no matter what, yes you can keep running them, I am talking practical usage. That also means, that from my perspective, the entire LLM industry can effectively rug pull us as consumers. Not just the frontier labs by raising pricing, but also the Chinese labs by simply no longer providing these models for free. We could hope they'd offer them for less than the frontier labs, but that is also not a given.

I honestly think it is better to be realistic about this. And to be extra clear, I am not coming at this from a perspective of someone against the use of LLMs in general. I happily use them in all sorts of tasks. I am also acutely

1.1 Avoiding GIMP's hole
The criticism of GIMP is historically true, and much of it still applies in 2026.

Bit depth.

GIMP's original core hard-coded 8-bit-per-channel tiles.
High bit depth needed a whole new engine, GEGL. GEGL began around 2000, was introduced as optional in 2.6 (2008), and the port only finished in GIMP 2.10 (2018), "the result of six years of work" on that port alone.
Only then did GIMP get 16/32-bit integer and float processing.
Non-destructive editing.

Photoshop has had adjustment layers since about 1994.
GIMP got non-destructive filters in 3.0 (March 2025), about seven years after 2.10 because of the GTK3 port.
It got non-destructive layer types (link layers, vector layers) in 3.2 (March 2026).
CMYK.

GIMP 3.x is still "a 100% RGB editor" internally.
CMYK exists only as export (JPEG/TIFF/PSD) and soft-proofing.
PSD.

Import is still lossy. Photoshop adjustment layers and most layer styles are not carried over faithfully, and text often needs re-typing.
3.2 converts legacy drop and inner shadows into GIMP filters, and added PSB export.


That isn't really isn't something you'd instruct the agent to if it were actually just does a transpilation. It's not like you can accidentally become GIMP doing that. You'd only need this when you're doing it from scratch and really, really don't want it to accidentally become GIMP.

text:
I mean, does that make it not true?

The industry is changing. These things don’t happen all at once or in every company according to a common timeline. Some people will feel the effects before others do, and that’s largely a matter of luck.

My SE career of 18 years ended last year when I and many in my department were unceremoniously laid off. I thought my department head was being unusually gruff when he gave me the bad news and bolted, only later did I learn that he’d been given the axe himself moments before, and his final duty with the company was to do the same to his subordinates. A shitty day all around. AI was never the stated reason, just nebulous “restructuring.” Okay. We were early adopters of Claude Code, so it was at least a factor, but saying more than that is idle speculation.

Anyway, I had already been grappling with career burnout for a few years. The work just wasn’t fun like it had been a decade before. It paid well, but (particularly after the pandemic killed off IRL coworker friendships and cool office perks) it was losing its luster. Then the introduction of Claude workflows redefined my role from a solution finder to a prompt-writer and AI babysitter. I was growing steadily less satisfied with that lot by the time the layoff came, and that was the final straw for me. Of course, I still had to look for new work.

When I re-entered the tech job market I noticed a lot of things were different from the last time I had been there:


Most of the roles now had “Agentic” or “AI-native” in the title. These were prompt-writing and AI babysitting jobs. Not what I ever signed up for or was good at.

Constant ghosting is apparently the norm now. Supposedly that’s because companies are overrun with LLM-slop applications and can’t sort the signal from the noise; also I guess a lot of job boards are now filled with fake ads and scams so the problem is multiplied. Very seldom did I hear back from any listing I applied to.

Pay on offer was notably reduced, across the board, from what I’d been making for years.

One of the things I’ve come to dread the most in job hunting life is the tech interview loop. I’ve been through too many to count, over the years, and have some real trauma from them. I’m not sure how the AI era has changed them, because I didn’t make it that far with anyone this time around. Felt like a slap in the face after all the years of hard work I’ve done.


Anyway to make a long story short, I pivoted. Left the tech sector entirely, and I’m happier for it. I got an administrative job at a large public university. Now I’m doing work that directly helps students. I meet with them and solve problems for them and I get to see the gratitude on their faces. I never got that from any of my old jobs, where I was kept as far away from humans as possible and the ultimate goal of every task I completed was just to make arrow go up.

I’m making about 1/4 of what I used to make, which legitimately sucks, but I’m happy with what I’m doing. Compared to constantly reviewing Claude’s verbose PRs, which were always so confident yet wrong in subtle but critical ways… this new job is mentally so much easier. And my non-technical coworkers think I’m a genius when I show them how to update their email signatures, lol. I feel appreciated, and for once like I might have lasting job security too.

A nice bonus is that I do have access to basically unlimited AI resources, courtesy of the university. So I’m able to keep up with the tech (which is still interesting to me) at no personal cost, and research uses for it on my own terms, to build things that help people, with no PMs breathing down my neck or KPIs driving everything I do. I’m pleased with how things worked out.

But, to summarize — I absolutely do credit AI’s impact on the tech industry as the killing blow to my SE career. I think maybe it hit me earlier than others (including those it’s still coming for but hasn’t reached yet), just because of the nature of my preexisting burnout and middle age long career history. I think many in the field will remain employed, but have to accept that the work they’re doing is irreversibly changing. Maybe they’ll like it better this way, I didn’t. I don’t know what the future holds for me or my SE compatriots, but I can say right now that I’m glad I got out.

The industry is full of people who don't know what they're doing and software robustness is a constant fight between the people who care about quality and the people who just want to say LGTM and merge. And that attitude stacks up technical debt that makes work harder in the future or bites you with a production incident.

Now that LLM usage is everywhere, that fight is getting harder. People throw PRs down faster, apparently look at and test them less, and more people are just rubber stamping them without looking at the chances. This is essentially shifting a massive amount of work onto more senior developers who are baby sitting more.

Just the other day I caught someone submitting a config file change with a unit test testing the configuration, and multiple other people approved the PR before I blocked it. Not testing the configuration loader/parser, which already had through tests; Claude made a new test file to test that the configuration changes were set as it expected. Seriously, you don't write code to test runtime configuration (which already has full coverage for the functionality the config drives).

Software quality is cooked, and the experience for end users is going to get much worse if this madness doesn't die down. And probably kill people as this affects cars, planes, heavy machinery, infrastructure, etc..

I'd hope medical device companies learned from THERAC-25, but hey, it's the future now. Let's just let Claude worry about it. /s
